entry.title: The Future Caught Up to the Past

link.title: The Future Caught Up to the Past

entry.content:
I have files from the golden age of home computers. Documents written in PFS First Choice, Microsoft Works, WordPerfect, early Microsoft Word, and CorelDraw. Formats from applications I had completely forgotten existed. I haven’t heard the name “Microsoft Works” in probably fifteen years.

These files survived every platform transition because of being organized, copying forward as one platform was discarded to the next. They outlasted the applications that created them. They outlasted the operating systems those applications ran on. They persisted, unopenable, through every transition.

And then the future showed up and read them.

The BBS Files

The oldest batch was the one I least expected to recover: ANSI animation files from bulletin board systems in the early ’90s.

In the pre-internet days, there were BBSes (Bulletin Board Systems). All the dial tones of the modem to dial up local numbers, back in the days of long-distance calling charges. One of my early technical hobbies was drawing ANSI animation files for BBSes, both mine and others. Hand-drawn character by character in TheDraw, animated frame by frame, these home screens greeted every caller who dialed in. I collaborated with friends who ran boards, and the home screen was everything.

I pointed Claude Code at the files. “These are ANSI animation files from TheDraw. Convert them to animated gifs.”

Claude identified the TheDraw format, parsed the ANSI escape codes for color and positioning, reconstructed the frame sequences, and converted them into animated GIFs. The color palette and frame timing were preserved. Screens I had not seen in over thirty years, rendered on a modern display. Old screen handles I had completely forgotten stared back at me. One was unmistakably a Douglas Adams reference. I must have been deep into The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy that year. I don’t remember choosing that handle. But the file does.

The Documents Nobody Can Open

After the BBS files, I turned to writing samples. High school essays. Undergraduate papers. Graduate coursework. Files spanning a decade of education, saved in formats that no modern application will touch.

The traditional recovery path is a project in itself. Hunt for conversion utilities. Hope they still exist. Upload personal documents to some random website offering free format conversion. Repeat for every file, every format, every era of software.

Instead, I gave Claude Code the folder. “Convert these to markdown.” Okay, it was quite a bit more complicated than that.

It identified the formats and converted the content. PFS First Choice, a DOS-era integrated suite, became clean markdown. WordPerfect documents with their proprietary formatting codes became structured text. Microsoft Works files came through intact. No hunting for converters. No uploading to unknown services.

But the actual process had its complications. Some files had Microsoft Equation Editor, which Microsoft locked down due to security issues; all attempts at conversion produced unacceptable results. Other files came through as sentence, line break, sentence rather than paragraph format, which required additional Claude Code instructions to correct. Claude Code also handled building the frontmatter details for long-term reference.

What the Old Files Show

The recovered documents are a timeline. Over 2,500 markdown files, organized by era and institution. High school writing is earnest and overwrought. Undergraduate work shows the first attempts at structured argument. Graduate writing is tighter, shaped by professors who would not tolerate filler.

None of it needs to be published. But it belongs in a system where I can find it and connect it to what came after. Converting to markdown and filing it in my vault means these documents are no longer trapped in amber. They are part of the personal experience.

That matters more than nostalgia. The patterns are visible. You can trace a line from a college essay about human-computer interaction to a career spent building systems at that exact intersection.

The Future Reflects the Past

The future caught up to the present to reflect the past.

The tools I have today can read files I created before those tools were imaginable. The AI that converts a PFS First Choice document into markdown was not conceivable when that document was written.

The part of AI that rarely gets discussed is not what it builds forward, but what it recovers from behind.

Every person accumulates a digital past. Files in dead formats. Creative work locked inside applications that no longer run. That accumulation used to represent permanent loss, measured in format obsolescence.

It doesn’t have to anymore. The future is not just catching up to the present. It is reaching back, reading what was left behind, and making it whole again.

entry.title: Claude Code + Obsidian: The Addiction Nobody Warned Me About

link.title: Claude Code + Obsidian: The Addiction Nobody Warned Me About

entry.content:
Imagine you wake up one morning and discover that elves have reorganized your basement.

Not the chaotic, well-intentioned kind that shove everything into unmarked boxes. These elves are meticulous. They sorted, labeled, and shelved every item. But here’s the part that makes them genuinely useful: before they touched anything, they asked you where it should go.

That’s what working with Claude Code inside an Obsidian vault feels like.

The Elves Ask Questions

The analogy holds up better than you’d expect. Claude Code does the heavy lifting, all of it, but it doesn’t operate in a vacuum. It asks. “Should this go under projects or areas?” “Do you want this frontmatter field populated?” “This Word doc has formatting quirks; here’s how I’d convert it. Does that match your convention?”

You provide the judgment. It provides the energy.

And when you come back to your vault, the work is done. Not half-done. Not “I made some progress and here’s a status update.” Done. Converted, formatted, linked, and filed according to the system you defined.

Bring Everything

This is where the addiction starts.

I had a folder of Word documents. Recipes, mostly. The kind of thing that accumulates over years because the format was good enough at the time. I pointed Claude Code at them and said, “Convert these to Obsidian markdown with my recipe template.”

It did. All of them. Proper frontmatter, consistent formatting, wikilinks where appropriate. The original .docx files became clean, searchable, linked notes inside my vault.

So naturally, I started looking around for more things to bring in.

That’s the hook. Once you see how fast structured data appears in your vault, you start scanning your digital life for anything that isn’t in Obsidian yet. Old documents. Clipped references. Notes from other tools. Everything becomes a candidate for migration because the cost of migration just dropped to nearly zero.

Organization Is Not the Bottleneck

I am an organized person. I will put that claim on the table without hesitation. My vault has a defined folder structure, consistent frontmatter conventions, a visibility system, linking patterns, and archive workflows. The system is not the problem.

The problem is energy.

Knowing exactly where something should go and how it should be formatted does not magically generate the hours needed to do it. Every knowledge worker has a backlog of “I know what this needs, I just haven’t gotten to it.” The gap between intention and execution is not a knowledge gap. It’s a capacity gap.

A personal AI doesn’t replace your organizational instincts. It gives those instincts the energy to actually execute.

That changes the math entirely. Instead of triaging what’s worth the effort to organize, you organize everything. Instead of leaving that stack of documents for “someday,” someday becomes today. The bottleneck shifts from execution to curation, and curation is the part you’re already good at.

Human in the Loop, Not Human in the Way

The pattern that emerges is surprisingly natural. Claude Code proposes. I approve, adjust, or redirect. It executes. I verify. The cycle is fast enough that it feels collaborative rather than supervisory.

This is not autopilot. I am making decisions at every step. But the decisions are the interesting ones: what should this be called, where does it belong, does this structure serve future me? The tedious parts, the file conversion, the frontmatter population, the bulk reformatting, those are handled.

It’s the difference between designing a room and carrying the furniture. Both require effort. Only one requires your taste.

Why It’s Addictive

The addiction isn’t about novelty. It’s about compound returns.

Every note that enters the vault properly formatted and linked makes the vault more useful. Every converted document eliminates a data silo. Every consistent piece of frontmatter makes future queries more powerful. The value of each individual action is small, but the cumulative effect transforms your knowledge base from a collection of files into an interconnected system.

And because the cost of each action dropped from “fifteen minutes of manual formatting” to “one sentence of instruction,” you do more of it. A lot more.

I used to make peace with the fact that some things would stay in their original format because conversion wasn’t worth the time. That compromise is gone now. The elves showed up, they asked where everything goes, and they got to work.

The digital-basement has never looked better.

entry.title: AI Doesn’t Have Motivation. You Do.

link.title: AI Doesn’t Have Motivation. You Do.

entry.content:
Here’s the thing nobody tells you about working with AI on a real project: it gets confused about 30% of the time.

It references older, outdated approaches. It forgets what you already established. It confidently presents something that contradicts a decision you made together three prompts ago.

And that 30% is the entire point.

The Result Is Only as Good as the Instruction

At the end of every session, the AI output was only as good as the instruction I gave it. Vague input produced vague results. Precise input, with clear patterns and explicit constraints, produced work I could actually use.

This isn’t a criticism of the technology. It’s an observation about the skill required to use it well. The gap between “AI can do this” and “AI did this well” is filled entirely by the human operating it.

Knowledge Curation Is the Real Work

Building a website with AI forced me into a role I didn’t expect: knowledge curator.

What should AI remember from our prior work? What should it forget? When it references something outdated, how do I correct course without losing momentum?

This is just knowledge curation. It’s the same discipline that applies to managing documentation, onboarding new team members, or maintaining institutional memory in any organization. The difference is that with AI, the feedback loop is faster and the cost of poor curation is immediate. You see the consequences of ambiguity in real time.

AI Has No Motivation

AI wouldn’t power up one morning and decide, “Let’s build a website for Michael today.” It needed human input. It needed direction, context, and judgment.

What it created, in combination with that human input, was something neither of us would have produced alone. Not a replacement. An augmentation.

I defined the goals. I made the architectural decisions. I caught the errors. AI handled the implementation velocity, the pattern translation, and the breadth of technical knowledge I hadn’t maintained in years.

The result: an augmented human who could ship a project that would have taken weeks in a fraction of the time.

The Bridge

This is the bridge I’m traveling right now. Learning what to delegate, what to verify, and what to keep in my own hands. Building the instinct for when AI is saving me time and when it’s leading me sideways.

That instinct doesn’t come from reading about AI. It comes from using it on real work, hitting the 30% failure rate, and developing the judgment to navigate it.

The technology will keep evolving. The skill of working with it is what compounds.

entry.title: Why I’m Building a Website in 2026 (And Why You Should Too)

link.title: Why I’m Building a Website in 2026 (And Why You Should Too)

entry.content:
I’ll be honest. I haven’t paid attention to front-end code in years. My specialization is data and backend automation; within corporate, my user interfaces are constrained by the automation tool’s development environment.

So when I decided to build a personal website on GitHub Pages, I knew I wasn’t going to sit down and hand-code every piece of it. I am going to use AI. The question is which AI, and how.

Your Experience May Vary

I have been using AI tools - but within use cases of documentation, refinement, and sometimes creativity. So - new project means new use cases that I began comparing across multiple AI platforms. The experiences were not equal.

Some tools were too agreeable. I’d get confident, well-structured answers that turned out to be wrong. It became a running joke with friends: “Yes, you’re right, let me check my work.” When your AI assistant agrees with everything you say and then quietly rewrites its own answer, trust erodes fast.

Other tools struggled with context. They would lose track of decisions we had already made, reference outdated approaches, or forget the architectural patterns we had established two prompts earlier. For example, yes, I really do want two spaces and the oxford comma in all of my work - it is a reflection of my deep appreciation for literature and readability.

The lesson: your experience with AI varies significantly based on the tool. Because of limitations and frustrations with some platforms, I kept seeking a better fit for my needs. That search led me to Claude Opus, which brings a different kind of confidence: not the “yes, you’re right” kind, but the “here’s why, and here’s what to watch out for” kind.

How the Relationship Evolves

At first, I used AI as a mentor coach. Simple questions:

  • I want to build a website on github.io. How do I do that?
  • What templates are available that meet my criteria?
  • How do I run this locally for faster feedback?

Then, as my trust increased, the collaboration deepened. I started asking architectural questions:

  • Timeline3 is designed for hardcoding events into JSON. How do we restructure this into a YAML and Liquid workflow?
  • This component assumes static data. How do we make it data-driven?

And here’s where it gets fun.

Separation of Data from Code

I haven’t been in front-end world for a while, so getting to see actual separation of data models from presentation is a great moment. YAML files for structured content, essentially simplified lists of items that are even more readable than JSON. Liquid templates that function like HTML on overdrive, with scripting and data binding built in.

The ability to throw together a YAML file, keep updating it as details evolve, and watch the site regenerate is genuinely satisfying. Don’t laugh, but seeing the current state of front-end tooling is a pleasant surprise.

AI as Co-Writer

Where I’ve ended up is that Claude is the co-writer of the process. I do not sit and code each piece of markup. Instead, I have to be clear in my communication, specify the pattern I want, and review what is provided.

This is a different skill than coding. It’s closer to technical direction. You’re not writing the implementation; you’re defining the intent and validating the output.

Credit Where It’s Due

I want to give a shoutout to the contributors behind the al-folio Jekyll template. They built a foundation that lets me start by simply swapping out Albert Einstein’s placeholder data with my own. That’s outstanding open-source work: giving others a running start.

And then my curiosity says, “and then what?” I knew I wanted timelines, so I found a working timeline solution. But it wasn’t in the format I needed. So I use Claude to translate it from one architecture to another.

That’s the pattern. Find a foundation someone else built. Learn from it. Extend it with AI as your co-developer. Mentorship doesn’t have to be in person; sometimes it’s the prior work that others left for you to build on.

entry.title: The EQ Side of AI
entry.content:
In a previous post, I argued that AI is a force multiplier, not a differentiator, and that good design determines whether AI systems actually work for people. But design alone is not sufficient. The critical element is still the human who connects other humans to interactive systems.

That requires emotional intelligence.

What EQ Actually Means in Practice

Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize and manage your own emotions, and to understand and respond appropriately to others. In management consulting the name Peter Drucker eventually appears, often associated with the idea that what gets measured gets improved. That applies to humans as well as machines.

Earlier this year I completed an EQ-i leadership assessment and coaching process with Parul Agarwal of Oralume. One of the surprising outcomes for me was not a weakness in problem solving or stress tolerance. I scored strongly in both. What the report highlighted instead was a tradeoff. When I rely heavily on that problem-solving mode, my patience for explanation can diminish.

After all, how many times do I need to explain that water is wet.

The value of the measurement was awareness. The metric itself becomes a tool. It helps me recognize when I need to slow down, communicate differently, and meet the listener where they are. In an interesting parallel, we often ask AI systems to verify their own work. The assessment functions similarly for people. It introduces a deliberate pause between reaction and response.

Why This Matters for AI

Those are exactly the abilities still required when working with AI. AI produces probabilities. A person must judge whether they make sense, explain them to others, and accept responsibility for acting on them.

Human-centric technology is not technology that replaces people. It is technology designed around how people think, decide, trust, and collaborate. AI multiplies capability. Design makes it usable. Emotional intelligence makes it responsible.

Organizations that combine all three will outperform those that rely on AI alone. The value of AI is not in what it produces, but in what people can responsibly do with it together.

entry.title: AI is not a Differentiator, It is a Force Multiplier

link.title: AI is not a Differentiator, It is a Force Multiplier

entry.content:
What differentiates a person, a product, or a company in 2026? It is not AI.

AI is a force multiplier.

In capable hands it reshapes organized work, just as earlier multipliers did: Roman road engineering, the medieval heavy plow and stirrup, the Renaissance printing press, the Industrial Age steam engine, the Modern Age adoption of electricity, and the Information Age transistor.

Human society existed before AI and will exist after it. The impact is practical, not apocalyptic. AI amplifies what already exists. A force multiplier allows the same number of people to produce greater outcomes by expanding effective power, productivity, and coordination.

The differentiator is not the technology. It is the human using it.

AI increases output, but it does not improve judgment. It does not understand context, intention, or consequence. Those come from people.

Design Determines Whether AI Actually Works

Good design determines whether a system can actually be used. As [Don Norman](https://a.co/d/05G9J4o2) explains, systems fail not because users are incompetent, but because the design does not communicate how the system works. AI systems are especially vulnerable to this. Early computing captured the same lesson in the phrase "garbage in, garbage out." When assumptions, data quality, and process safeguards are weak, the output may be precise yet wrong.

AI and ML systems do not understand truth. They detect patterns and predict outcomes. Biased, incomplete, mislabeled, or contextually incorrect data produces confident errors. A large portion of my career has involved troubleshooting technology implementations where the real problem was not the software but the gap between system behavior and human expectation.

An organization may deploy powerful models, yet if outcomes confuse users, especially users who question results, trust does not form. This becomes even more critical when agentic systems operate autonomously without human judgment. At that point the value collapses. The problem is not the model. The problem is the human experience around the model.

AI is Quietly Improving Design

A positive side effect of the current AI investment cycle is renewed attention to design. Agents, agentic workflows, MCP, and even the return of the CLI increase transparency. They reveal the actions a system actually allows and the clues showing how to interact with it. In many ways we are moving beyond the limitations of the purely mouse-driven UI toward interfaces that better express system capability.

Don Norman’s The Design of Everyday Things influenced me years ago, and it remains highly relevant for anyone building products or technology.

Design, however, is not sufficient by itself. The critical element is still the human who connects other humans to interactive systems. Not the IQ of model builders, but the EQ of the people guiding how AI is used as a multiplier.

I explore that idea further in a companion post: The EQ Side of AI.

entry.title: International Lego Day
entry.content:
Sending tactile block greetings to my fellow AI and automation leaders on International LEGO Day of Play 2026. When your occupation lives in abstract systems, data models, and digital workflows, building something physical reinforces core product truths. Constraints matter. Interfaces matter. Small design decisions compound into durable outcomes.

Stepping away from the screen to build with our hands sharpens how we think about core structures, modularity, feedback loops, iteration, and user experience. Sometimes the clearest product solutions come from snapping a few bricks together and watching what believably holds.

The photo is a work-in-progress incorporating new elevations and lighting for the Botanical Garden (21353) and Motorized Lighthouse (21335). Just like automation, you need to know where you’re going in order to plan ahead to get there with accuracy!

entry.title: Why I’m Building a Website in 2026 (And Why You Should Too)

link.title: Why I’m Building a Website in 2026 (And Why You Should Too)

entry.content:
It has been years since I actually built a website. I came up in the era of the first browser wars, when your biggest design decision was whether to bold the font or blink it. Then CSS arrived, then e-commerce engines, then persona tracking platforms like Sitecore. My career drifted toward back-office technologies, and I stopped thinking about front-end work entirely.

But here’s the problem with spending 25 years in enterprise automation: most of what you accomplish gets filtered through NDAs and proprietary technology. Your best work becomes invisible. You can talk about the outcomes, but the substance belongs to someone else.

So I made a decision. It is time to decouple my personal identity from my corporate identity.

Treating Yourself Like a Product

The key to any product development, including yourself, is setting clear target goals. What are you trying to accomplish?

My current target is reaching expert-level proficiency in terminal-based AI workflows. I believe the landscape will look completely different by 2028, but that’s a topic for a future post.

You might ask what terminal AI has to do with building a website. Fair question. Here’s the connection: it’s the same product management discipline I’ve applied for decades. You define the destination, break it into discrete phases, and adapt along the way.

My roadmap looks something like this:

  • Build an online presence and establish a market differential. Know what to share and what to keep private.
  • Get organized first. Local files, notes, and knowledge management have to be in order before anything goes public. That means investing in tools like a Synology NAS, Directory Opus, and Obsidian vaults.
  • Upskill deliberately. Learn Markdown deeply. Be able to describe the practical differences between AI platforms. Combine those tools in the terminal to automate the repetitive copy-and-paste workflows.
  • Approach it with a security mindset. Run local as much as possible. Any cloud-based tools must be isolated with human controls.
  • Stay cost-conscious. Avoid long-term subscription fatigue. Every recurring cost needs to justify itself.
  • Plan for legacy. How does this knowledge transfer to the next generation?

That last one catches people off guard. But if you’re building a personal knowledge system, the question of what happens to it after you matters - especially when your legacy is not rooted in applied technology.

The Point

None of this is complicated. It’s just discipline. The same phased approach that works for enterprise product launches works for reinventing your professional presence.

Define the target. Break it into phases. Adapt along the way.

The website is just the first deliverable. The real product is the system behind it.
